hook: A city will replace its old water pipes only if a test finds convincing evidence that more than 10% of homes have too much lead. The test can go wrong in two ways: the city spends millions on pipes it did not need, or it leaves families drinking unsafe water. Which mistake is worse, and how can the city make it less likely?

prereq.q: A test at $\alpha = 0.05$ gives a p-value of 0.03. What is the decision?
prereq.why: Reject $H_0$ when the p-value is less than $\alpha$.

prereq.q: If $\hat{p}$ is approximately normal with mean 0.60 and standard deviation 0.0346, which expression gives $P(\hat{p} \ge 0.558)$?
prereq.why: Standardize the boundary with the distribution's own mean and standard deviation, and keep the direction.

figure.caption: The null distribution (p = 0.5) and one alternative (p = 0.60) for samples of 200, with the rejection cutoff: α under the null curve, β and power under the alternative.

chain.cause: $H_0$ is true but the sample happens to look extreme
chain.effect: the test rejects $H_0$: a Type I error, with probability $\alpha$

chain.cause: $H_a$ is true but the sample happens to look ordinary
chain.effect: the test fails to reject $H_0$: a Type II error, with probability $\beta$

chain.cause: A specific alternative value is true
chain.effect: the test rejects $H_0$ with probability power $= 1 - \beta$

chain.cause: The sample size grows (or $\alpha$ grows, or the true value is farther from $p_0$)
chain.effect: the curves overlap less or the cutoff is easier to pass, so power rises and $\beta$ falls

ideas: Type I: $H_0$ true, but we reject it (a false alarm). Probability $\alpha$.
Type II: $H_a$ true, but we fail to reject $H_0$ (a missed effect). Probability $\beta$, which depends on the true value.
Describe an error with the condition first: "if the true proportion of all __ is __, but we find (do not find) convincing evidence that ...", then the consequence in context.
Power $= 1 - \beta$: the probability of rejecting $H_0$ when a specific alternative is true.
More power: larger $n$ (best), larger $\alpha$, or a true value farther from $p_0$. For a fixed $n$, lowering $\alpha$ raises $\beta$.

misconception.wrong: A Type I error is when the test gets the answer wrong, and a Type II error is when it gets it wrong a second time.
misconception.right: Each is a specific mistake: Type I rejects a true $H_0$; Type II fails to reject a false $H_0$. After a rejection only a Type I error is possible; after a failure to reject, only a Type II error.

summary: A Type I error rejects a true $H_0$ (probability $\alpha$); a Type II error fails to reject a false $H_0$ (probability $\beta$, against a specific alternative). Describe each with the condition first and its consequence in context. Power $= 1 - \beta$ is the chance of detecting a real effect; it grows with the sample size, with $\alpha$, and with the distance between the true value and $p_0$.
